messages.subject: Habitat - Population Density Relationship in Distance
messages.subject_clean: Habitat - Population Density Relationship in Distance
messages.body_plain:
Hello everybody,

I am quite new with using distance and I believe it will be a powerful tool to analyze my dataset.

Basically I've been doing field survey for the past 7 weeks on a chameleon population in an Aegan island.

The study is designed that way :   -  4 habitat   - 3 transects of 700m each per habitat (12 transects in total)  - all transect have been investigated 6 times

I want to run a ds() with comparison of population density between my 4 habitats (i.e : stratum)

First of all I wanted to know how to properly enter the dataset to analyse it in Rstudio (you'll find a really basic one in attached files).
 I believe that my region study should be my 4 different habitats - but when i follow the code to conduct simple distance analysis with stratified study region (from the minke whales data), none of the models fit.

For the moment I'm just looking forward a proper and consistent way to analyze my data set.

Thank you in advance for any kind of help.

Bests regards,

Etienne P.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Habitat - Population Density Relationship in Distance
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Habitat - Population Density Relationship in Distance
messages.body_plain:
Etienne

Welcome to the world of distance sampling.

There are two principles to keep in mind when organising your data for use with Distance or ds().  First, respect your survey design.  Your design is hierarchical: you have 4 strata and *within* each strata, you have 3 transects.  It would be easiest for you (and for the software) to sort your data first by stratum, then by transect within stratum.  That keeps all sightings made in a stratum together, and all sightings on a transect together.

Second principle is to record effort on transects were there were no sightings.  The data file you attached showed only the 29 sightings you made.  The numbering of the transects is hard for me to understand, but I suspect there were several transects on which no chameleons were detected.  Those should also appear in the datafile used by ds().

If you have been using the minke dataset (http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/minke.csv) as an example, note all the data for the southern stratum appears first, with transects within that stratum appearing in sequence.  Particularly notice transects 5,6,9,10,11,12: their lengths were recorded, but the perpendicular distance field is blank, because there were no sightings on those transects.

As a final comment, you note each transect was 700m in length and each were walked 6 times.  In that case, the total effort associated with each transect should be 4200m (or 420000cm) rather than the value '70000' you have in your file.  I also note there were no chameleons in your data set detected >240 units (cm) from the transect; that could be troublesome as an assumption of distance sampling is that all animals on the transect are seen and that detectability diminishes as distance from the transect.

messages.subject: (Approximately) repeated survey transects from ships of opportunity
messages.subject_clean: (Approximately) repeated survey transects from ships of opportunity
messages.body_plain:
Hello Group,

I'm interested in using DS and DSM methods applied to a data set of marine mammal surveys undertaken on ships of opportunity (SOO). The SOO travels up and down a bay over the course of a day. Below is a snapshot of the SOO tracks over the course of 1 day (top) and 1 week (bottom) during which observers were on-effort.  I have data from surveys much like these over many weeks each summer of many years. I'm trying to decide the best practice regarding what to consider a unique transect vs a repeat of a transect already run. The distance between a track going up and a track going down the bay ranges from approx. 0m to approx 1,500m. From previous posts on this topic, I understand that for transects repeated (in exactly the same location) should be addressed by multiplying the length of the transect by the number of times it was surveyed to serve as the effort metric. I wonder if in my situation the total length of closely spaced transects (though they are not exact overlaps) over some time period (perhaps a week) should all be added together to be considered the effort?

Any thoughts are greatly appreciated,
Sara

messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am trying to compare density estimates between two count surveys using equation 3.102 in page 85 (Buckland et al., 2001). My problem is that in each survey I got more than one plausible model (delta AIC < 2). For these reason I am using model averaging en each case. In this case is there any way to deal with this situation and compare model averaged densities between surveys?

Thanks in advance for any help

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Z-test for comparison between two surveys with multiple plausible models
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Z-test for comparison between two surveys with multiple plausible models
messages.body_plain:
Sergio

I presume you are performing your model-averaging by using a bootstrap and permitting Distance to choose among models for each bootstrap replicate (as described in Chapter 8 of the Users Guide).  In this case, the standard error reported in the output will contain model uncertainty.  Convert the standard errors for each of your surveys into variances by squaring, and use formula 3.99 to estimate the variance of the difference in the density estimates, and use 3.102 in the normal way.  In essence, you will perform your contrast of density estimates in the usual way.

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Z-test for comparison between two surveys with multiple plausible models
messages.body_plain:
Dear Eric,

Thanks for your message. Actually for my second survey I got some CDS and MCDS (multiple-covariates) models with delta AIC < 2, although point estimates are very close to each other as my potential covariates were uninformative based on their CIs including the zero value. So, for model averaging I am using instead function model.average from RMark package based on equation 4.1 from Burnham and Anderson (2002) along with tail area 95% confidence intervals as described by Turek and Fletcher (2012).

This function also gives me standard errors SE and I already squared them to get variances and finally applied equation 3.102 to get the z-score. The test was significant with a z = 2.71 and p < 0.01. I am quite confused at this point as there is a big amount of interception in 95% confidence intervals between surveys densities.

Here are my model averaging results:
SURVEY 1:  D = 0.043, SE = 7.405E-03, VAR = 5.483E-05, 95%CI = 0.028-0.058
SURVEY 2:  D = 0.035, SE = 6.797E-03 , VAR = 4.620E-05, 95%CI = 0.022-0.048

This interception between CIs seems to be incongruent with the z-test results, isn´t it?

Thanks

Sergio

You are right to be suspicious that your results seem inconsistent.  I performed your calculations for the z-test (Eqn. 3.102) with these simple lines of code
> se1 <- 7.405e-3
> se2 <- 6.797e-3
> d1 <- .043
> d2 <- .035
> num <- d1-d2
> den <- sqrt(se1^2 + se2^2)
> num/den
[1] 0.7958988

and did not get 2.71 as you did.

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] (Approximately) repeated survey transects from ships of opportunity
messages.body_plain:
Sara

Because you will be using model-based rather than design-based inference (because of non-random transect placement) for your Glacier Bay study, the meaningful measure of effort is actually the size of the segments rather than the lengths of the transects.

If you look at the NOAA research cruises in the Gulf of Mexico used in the Miller et al. (2013) MEE paper,

you will notice some "nearly" repeated transects in those surveys.  We segmented each transect separately, whether atop other transects, or nearly so.  Hope that's helpful.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Matthew,

I am not exactly sure what was going on when you were trying to create the coverage grid with the coordinate system and projection defined. When I looked at your study area and strata they appeared to be in metres.

The easiest thing to do, as you have done, is project your shapefiles outside Distance. Then Distance in fact doesn't need to know anymore than what units the shapefiles are in and this makes life a lot simpler. I think Distance got confused somehow with the coordinates and projections. I found it strange that even when I removed your .prj files Distance was still concerned about coordinate systems.

I therefore created a new project and added a strata layer with 5 strata. I then closed the project and copied the shapefile files across the ones that Distance had created. BUT I only copied the .shp, .shx and .dbf files. I did NOT include any other parts of the shapefile. Store the .prj somewhere so you can project back but Distance doesn't need to know about it. Distance then created a coverage grid without issue.

Hope this helps,

Kind Regards,

Laura

Dr. L. Marshall
Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
University of St. Andrews

More specifically I am having problems with preparing a coverage layer in Distance that adopts a matching projected coordinate system to that of the parent and child layers.  In my study I have chosen to use line transects to sample a target butterfly population across a relatively modest area (approximately 2.5 km2) comprised of multiple fields of state managed grasslands here in the eastern USA.  I’m using Distance 6.2 Release 1 on Windows 7 via the Parallels 10 for Mac application.
>
> I have imported shapefiles for the global and strata layers by copying them into the project folder and I am able to prepare maps of these in Distance and ensure that everything looks correct.  By checking the “Data Layer Properties” window in Distance I can see that the Geographic Coordinate System for the global layer is: NAD 1983 NSRS2007 UTM Zone 18N and this differs only slightly for the Strata layer: NAD 1983 UTM Zone 18N.  The projection for both layers is the Transverse Mercator and the units have been set to “meters”.  When adding these two layers to a map in Distance I find that they overlap perfectly, just as intended.
>
> When I attempt to add a coverage layer, there seems to be a problem with getting the geographic coordinate system for all layers to match.  After creating the coverage layer and attempting to map it, I find that the specified grid does not fall overtop the global and strata layers and the points end up distributed wildly in space.  When I “zoom to extent” with all 3 layers selected only a single point comes into view and the global and strata layers are then no longer visible.  After checking the layer properties for the coverage layer in Distance again it seems that the geographic coordinate system and projection are largely the same (i.e. North American 1983 with all the appropriate corresponding Projection Parameters) but only the Zone, 18N hasn’t been specified.  Furthermore there is no projected coordinate system specified in the first line of the coordinate system information that appears when clicking on the "Geographic data" tab of the Data Layer Properties dialogue. I have double-checked and ensured that the shapefile units for all layers have been set to meters.
>

Firstly I have been able to prepare otherwise meaningful designs for the study by ensuring that the Geographic Coordinate System and Projection are set to “None” for all layers including by also setting the coordinate system to “none” by using the “Project Properties” menu.  I am able to experiment with different designs and calculate coverage probability statistics for each one without any problems.  In fact based on the results of these explorations I feel that I have identified an otherwise suitable design for the study yet when I attempt to map the sampler starting and end points in ArcMap I am unable to do so.  So my first question is, “Is there is a way to work backward and convert these simple linear coordinates to the appropriate coordinate system using the results of the survey design engine when geographic coordinate system has been set to “none”?  I sense that the answer to this question is probably “no” although if it provides a solution, of course that is all that I’m after.  That being said, if as a solution this approach is more complex than getting the coordinate system of the coverage layer to correspond correctly to the geo-referenced global and child layers I’d rather keep things as simple as possible and run the designs again in Distance with a geocoordinate system that translates correctly across all layers.

After doing the and attempting to create the coverage layer the warning message, “No points fell within the survey area” appears.  Although this doesn’t seem possible I have changed the spacing between grid points to as low as a few meters, just for the sake of argument, but the software returns the same warning message.

The coverage layer that is created does not overlay the global and strata layers and the grid points are spread wildly in space as before.
>
> I have done my best to research the archives on the issue and although there are some relevant posts where users encountered the same problem where none of their grid points fell within their survey areas, none of these have solved my problem.  I’m aware that in the Distance user’s manual the authors advise that in some cases geometry problems are responsible for the design engine responding strangely, however I have been unable to link to the appropriate page on the ESRI website where these issues are addressed at greater length.  Furthermore, I suspect this is not the problem I’m having since my global and strata layers map correctly by themselves.
>
> In any case, if anyone can please advise me on this problem and coming up with a solution, I would really appreciate it.  We're so eager to adopt a design for this study and start implementing it in the field!
>

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Distribution of density estimate?
messages.body_plain:
Sam

Here is an answer that is a joint effort including a contribution from Dr Rachel Fewster at Univ of Auckland in NZ.  First Dr. Fewster's comments:

One interpretation is that you are asking how Distance converts from variance estimates to confidence intervals.  If you are using analytic variance estimates, they are obtained using a few different steps for different components of the variance: the components correspond to encounter rate, detection probability, and mean group size.  An in-depth description is given in the attached paper, which also outlines what "variance" means in a conceptual sense: see Section 2.

Having obtained the analytic variance estimates, Distance then converts these to confidence intervals using an assumption that estimates of N or D follow a log-Normal distribution, with a bit of extra leeway added through the "df" term.  The details of this step are given in the Screenshot snippet attached, with a bit of extra detail in Section 7 of the paper, both of which also point to the corresponding references in the 2001 Intro Distance Sampling book (page 77). The justification of the log-Normal distribution is more complicated, but it can be found in Fewster & Jupp, Biometrika, 2009.

Another possible interpretation is that you are using bootstrap variance estimates, and you are just asking how you can access the distribution of estimates obtained in each bootstrap replicate.  (This is where ER steps in below).

A third interpretation is that you're asking about the conceptual distribution of repeated surveys that creates what we call "variance" in the first place.  This is described in Section 2 of the Fewster et al. (2009) attached, as mentioned above.
---

Regarding performing bootstrapping in Distance to create sampling distributions of statistics and parameter estimates, I've written a small note on this subject that you can find at this link

https://www.dropbox.com/s/7jedjeqqodybwg2/distance-bootstrap-file-summary.pdf?dl=0

This involves creating a "stats" file in Distance, then summarising the contents of that file in R.  The Rmarkdown source file that created my note is at this link:
https://www.dropbox.com/s/5d3u3lq1yjvusz3/distance-bootstrap-file-summary.Rmd?dl=0

Hopefully that addresses your questions.

Hello distance samplers!

We are very pleased to inform you that new versions of our R packages
are now available on CRAN.

* For conducting "simple" CDS/MCDS analyses and estimating abundance:
  - Distance (0.9.6)  https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/Distance/index.html

* For analysing double observer surveys:
  - mrds (2.1.16)  https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/mrds/index.html

* For modelling spatially explicit distance sampling data:
  - dsm (2.2.12)  https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dsm/index.html

* For simulation of spatially explicit distance data:
  - DSsim (1.0.6)  https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/DSsim/index.html

* To deal with multiple species and identification uncertainty:
  - mads (0.1.4)  https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/mads/index.html

The NEWS files available at each of the above links contain details of
the updates to each package. We highly recommend you update your
versions using update.packages() in R to ensure you have the latest bug
fixes.

If you find any more bugs, these can be reported via github at
https://github.com/DistanceDevelopment/[package <https://github.com/DistanceDevelopment/%5Bpackage> name]/issues for each
package.

These packages will be included in the forthcoming release of Distance
for Windows.

We'd like to thank everyone who submitted a bug report to our packages
over the past year -- your reports make the software better for everyone.

Best wishes,
The Distance Development Team

Centre for Research into Ecological & Environmental Modelling

University of St. Andrews

messages.body_plain:
On Sunday, August 21, 2016 at 4:21:11 PM UTC-5, Len Thomas wrote:
> I agree with Eric -- it's almost certainly the apostrophe that is causing the problem.  If that's the case the workaround would be to remove it.  I also recommend you submit this as a bug to
> https://github.com/DistanceDevelopment/distance-bugs/issues
> -- we should be screening for this and throwing a helpful error message, at the least.
>
> Cheers, Len Thomas

You both were correct! I don't know why it didn't cross my mind to check for that.  The analysis ran smoothly after I took out the apostrophe.  I will report the bug as you suggested.
Thank you so much.
Beth
